question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

TACITURN
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Reticent.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Taciturn (adjective) means saying very little, habitually silent and reserved in speech. (मितभाषी, कम बोलने वाला)
◦ Example: The taciturn watchman answered every question with a nod.

 

• Reticent carries the same sense — unwilling to speak or to reveal one’s thoughts. (संकोची, कम बोलने वाला)
◦ Example: She remained reticent about her reasons for resigning.

 

• The Latin root tacere (“to be silent”) also gives us tacit (understood without being spoken). Spotting the root is the quickest route to the answer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Garrulous (बड़बोला): excessively talkative, especially about trivial matters — the exact opposite of taciturn.

 

• Option 3: Boisterous (उड्दंड, शोरगुल करने वाला): noisy, energetic and rough in behaviour.

 

• Option 4: Gregarious (मिलनसार): fond of company, sociable — again an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of taciturn often asked in SSC: laconic, reserved, tight-lipped, uncommunicative, withdrawn.

 

• Antonyms: loquacious, voluble, garrulous, chatty, effusive.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To steal someone’s thunder
option_1: To take the credit or attention that another person expected
option_2: To criticise a rival openly and without warning
option_3: To make a sudden and unexpected profit
option_4: To frighten an opponent into withdrawing
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To take the credit or attention that another person expected.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• “To steal someone’s thunder” means to win praise, credit or attention for oneself by doing first what another person had planned to do. (किसी का श्रेय या ध्यान छीन लेना)
◦ Example: By announcing the scheme a day early, the minister stole the mayor’s thunder.

 

• The idiom comes from the dramatist John Dennis, who invented a device for producing stage thunder; when his play failed and a rival company used his device, he is said to have complained that they had stolen his thunder.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 describes an attack in public, for which the idiom would be “to call someone out”.

 

• Option 3 describes an unexpected gain — that is “a windfall”, not stolen thunder.

 

• Option 4 describes intimidation; the idiom involves credit, not fear.

 

NOTE

 

• Related idioms worth revising: to take a leaf out of someone’s book (to imitate), to blow one’s own trumpet (to boast), to be in the limelight (to receive public attention).

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

EPHEMERAL
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Enduring.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ephemeral (adjective) means lasting for a very short time; short-lived. (क्षणभंगुर, अल्पकालिक)
◦ Example: Fame on social media is often ephemeral.

 

• Enduring means continuing or lasting over a long period, and is therefore its direct opposite. (चिरस्थायी, स्थायी)
◦ Example: The treaty created an enduring peace between the two states.

 

• The word comes from Greek ephemeros — “lasting only a day” — the same root as the insect ephemera (mayflies), which live for barely a day.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Transient (क्षणिक): passing quickly — a synonym, not an antonym.

 

• Option 3: Fleeting (क्षणभंगुर): lasting only a moment — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Momentary (क्षणिक): lasting for a moment — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Three of the four options here are synonyms of the given word. In antonym questions, first group the options that agree with one another; the odd one out is almost always the answer.

 

• Other antonyms of ephemeral: perennial, perpetual, everlasting, abiding, permanent.

question: Identify the misspelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Occurence.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is OCCURRENCE — with double ‘c’, double ‘r’ and the ending -ence (not -ance). It means an incident or event. (घटना)
◦ Example: Power failures are a daily occurrence in the area.

 

• The doubling rule explains it: occur is stressed on the last syllable, so the final r doubles before the suffix — occur → occurred, occurring, occurrence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Perseverance (लगन, धैर्य): steady persistence in a course of action — correctly spelt (-verance, not -verence).

 

• Option 2: Millennium (सहस्राब्दी): a period of a thousand years — correctly spelt (double l, double n, from Latin mille + annus).

 

• Option 4: Embarrassment (शर्मिंदगी): a feeling of self-conscious shame — correctly spelt (double r, double s).

 

NOTE

 

• High-frequency SSC spelling traps of the same family: occasion (double c, single s), accommodation (double c, double m), necessary (single c, double s), harassment (single r, double s).

question: Spot the correct spelling of the adjective meaning ‘relating to the sense of smell’.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Olfactory.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Olfactory (adjective) means connected with the sense of smell. (घ्राण संबंधी)
◦ Example: The olfactory nerve carries signals of smell to the brain.

 

• The word is built from Latin olere (to smell) + facere (to make), which fixes the sequence ol- → fact → -ory. The ending is -ory (as in auditory, gustatory, sensory), never -ary.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Olfactary — wrong ending; adjectives of this family take -ory.

 

• Option 2: Olefactory — an extra ‘e’ has been inserted after ol-.

 

• Option 4: Olphactory — the ‘ph’ is spurious; the root has a plain f.

 

NOTE

 

• Learn the five senses as a set: olfactory (smell), gustatory (taste), auditory (hearing), tactile (touch) and visual/optical (sight). SSC repeatedly tests their spellings.

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

‘The act of ending the life of a person suffering from an incurable disease, in order to relieve pain’
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Euthanasia.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Euthanasia means the painless ending of the life of a person who is suffering from an incurable and painful disease, often called mercy killing. (इच्छामृत्यु, दयामृत्यु)
◦ Example: The court laid down strict conditions under which passive euthanasia may be permitted.

 

• The word comes from Greek eu (good, easy) + thanatos (death) — literally “a good death”, which is exactly the sense of relief from suffering given in the expression.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Genocide (नरसंहार): the deliberate killing of a large group belonging to a particular nation, race or religion.

 

• Option 3: Homicide (हत्या): the killing of one human being by another — a general legal term with no element of mercy.

 

• Option 4: Infanticide (शिशु हत्या): the killing of an infant.

 

NOTE

 

• The Latin suffix -cide means “killing”. Revise the family together: patricide (father), matricide (mother), fratricide (brother), regicide (king), suicide (oneself).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

‘An intense dislike or fear of foreigners or strangers’
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Xenophobia.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Xenophobia means a deep dislike, distrust or fear of people from other countries or of anything foreign. (विदेशियों से घृणा या भय)
◦ Example: The riots were driven by xenophobia rather than by any real economic grievance.

 

• It is formed from Greek xenos (stranger, foreigner) + phobos (fear). The same root gives xenophile (a person fond of foreign people and customs).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Agoraphobia (खुले स्थानों का भय): fear of open or public places and crowds (agora = marketplace).

 

• Option 3: Acrophobia (ऊँचाई का भय): fear of heights (akron = peak).

 

• Option 4: Nyctophobia (अंधेरे का भय): fear of darkness or of the night (nyx = night).

 

NOTE

 

• Other phobias frequently asked: claustrophobia (enclosed spaces), hydrophobia (water), arachnophobia (spiders), hemophobia (blood), thanatophobia (death).

question:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.

 

Only after the audit had been completed ____ the discrepancy in the accounts.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. did the board notice.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When a sentence begins with a restrictive or negative adverbial such as Only after, Only when, Not until, Never, Seldom, Rarely, Hardly, No sooner, the main clause must be inverted — that is, it takes the question order: auxiliary + subject + main verb.

 

• Here the main clause is the board noticed the discrepancy. Inverted, it becomes did the board notice — the auxiliary did carries the past tense, so the main verb returns to its base form notice.
◦ Example: Only after the results were declared did she reveal her decision.

 

• Note that the inversion applies to the main clause, never to the adverbial clause itself (Only after the audit had been completed stays in normal order).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: ‘the board noticed’ keeps normal statement order and therefore ignores the compulsory inversion.

 

• Option 3: ‘the board did notice’ uses the emphatic did but still places the subject before the auxiliary, so it is not inverted.

 

• Option 4: ‘had the board noticed’ is inverted, but the past perfect is already used in the first clause; the second action must follow it in the simple past.

 

NOTE

 

• Remember the pairs that SSC tests every year: No sooner … than, Hardly/Scarcely … when, Not until … + inversion, Only if/when/after … + inversion.

question:
Select the correct option to fill in the blank.

 

Had the engineers inspected the foundation in time, the collapse ____ altogether.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. could have been avoided.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence opens with “Had the engineers inspected …”, which is the inverted form of the third conditional (If the engineers had inspected …). It refers to a past event that did not happen.

 

• The third conditional demands the structure: If + past perfect … would/could/might + have + V3. The main clause must therefore be could have been avoided (passive, because the collapse is the thing acted upon).
◦ Example: Had the warning been heeded, the loss could have been prevented.

 

• In this inverted pattern the word if is dropped and had moves to the front; the meaning is unchanged.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: ‘can be avoided’ is present tense and contradicts the past, unreal situation.

 

• Option 3: ‘would be avoided’ belongs to the second conditional (present/future unreal), not the third.

 

• Option 4: ‘will have been avoided’ is future perfect and cannot describe an event that is already over.

 

NOTE

 

• Inverted conditionals to memorise: Had I known … (= If I had known), Were I you … (= If I were you), Should you need help … (= If you should need help).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

One of the most persuasive argument (1)/ advanced by the committee (2)/ was that the subsidy had never reached (3)/ the intended beneficiaries. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (1).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The structure ‘one of the + superlative + noun’ always requires a plural noun, because one is being picked out from a group. The correct form is “One of the most persuasive arguments”.
◦ Example: He is one of the finest players in the league.

 

• Note the balance carefully: the noun after ‘one of the’ is plural, but the verb agreeing with ‘one’ is singular — which is why was in part (3) is perfectly correct here.

 

• Corrected sentence: One of the most persuasive arguments advanced by the committee was that the subsidy had never reached the intended beneficiaries.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (2) is correct: advanced by the committee is a reduced passive participle phrase modifying arguments.

 

• Part (3) is correct: the singular verb was agrees with one, and the past perfect had never reached correctly marks the earlier action.

 

• Part (4) is correct: the intended beneficiaries is a well-formed noun phrase.

 

NOTE

 

• Watch the two related traps: ‘one of the + plural noun + singular verb’, but ‘one of the + plural noun + who/that + plural verb’ — as in He is one of those students who are always punctual.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

Having examined the samples carefully (1)/ the conclusion was drawn (2)/ that the contamination had occurred (3)/ during transportation. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A sentence beginning with a participial phrase (Having examined …) must be followed immediately by the doer of that action. Here the phrase is left dangling, because the subject that follows is the conclusion — and a conclusion cannot examine samples.

 

• The error therefore lies in part (2), where the passive construction removes the human agent. The correction is to supply the logical subject:
◦ Corrected: Having examined the samples carefully, the researchers drew the conclusion that the contamination had occurred during transportation.

 

• Part (1) itself is grammatically well formed; it becomes faulty only because of what part (2) puts after it — and in such questions the part containing the mismatched subject is marked as the error.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (3) is correct: the past perfect had occurred rightly shows an action earlier than the drawing of the conclusion.

 

• Part (4) is correct: during transportation is an appropriate prepositional phrase of time.

 

• The same fault appears in the familiar example: Walking down the road, a snake crossed my path — as written, the snake is walking.

 

NOTE

 

• Rule of thumb: whenever a sentence opens with -ing or -ed/having + V3, check the very next noun. If that noun cannot perform the action, the modifier is dangling.

question:
Change the following sentence from active voice to passive voice.

 

The volunteers are distributing relief material among the flood-affected families.
option_1: Relief material is distributed among the flood-affected families by the volunteers.
option_2: Relief material is being distributed among the flood-affected families by the volunteers.
option_3: Relief material has been distributed among the flood-affected families by the volunteers.
option_4: Relief material was being distributed among the flood-affected families by the volunteers.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Relief material is being distributed among the flood-affected families by the volunteers.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The active sentence is in the present continuous tense (are distributing). The passive of the present continuous is formed as:
◦ Object + is/are + being + V3 + by + subject.

 

• Applying the rule step by step:
◦ Object relief material (uncountable, singular) becomes the subject → takes is;
◦ are distributing → is being distributed;
◦ the original subject the volunteers moves to the end with by.

 

• The tense of the original sentence must be preserved in the passive — this single check eliminates three of the four options.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is the passive of the simple present (The volunteers distribute …).

 

• Option 3 is the passive of the present perfect (The volunteers have distributed …).

 

• Option 4 is the passive of the past continuous (The volunteers were distributing …).

 

NOTE

 

• Continuous tenses in the passive always insert being: is/are being done, was/were being done. Perfect tenses insert been: has/have been done, had been done.

question:
Convert the sentence given below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

It is being alleged by the residents that the contractor used substandard material.
option_1: The residents alleged that the contractor used substandard material.
option_2: The residents are alleging that the contractor used substandard material.
option_3: It was alleged that substandard material had been used by the contractor.
option_4: Substandard material is being alleged by the residents.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The residents are alleging that the contractor used substandard material.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the impersonal passive ‘It is being alleged by X that …’, the real doer is the agent introduced by by — here the residents. In the active voice this agent becomes the subject.

 

• The passive verb is being alleged is in the present continuous, so the active verb must also be present continuous → are alleging (plural, agreeing with the residents).

 

• The that-clause is the object of the verb and is carried over unchanged: that the contractor used substandard material.
◦ Active: The residents are alleging that the contractor used substandard material.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 shifts the tense to the simple past (alleged), which the original does not permit.

 

• Option 3 is still passive and also changes the tense; the question asks for the active voice.

 

• Option 4 drops the that-clause entirely and distorts the meaning — it is the allegation, not the material, that is being made.

 

NOTE

 

• Impersonal passives such as It is said/believed/reported/alleged that … convert to the active as People say/believe/report that …, or, when an agent is named with by, that named agent becomes the subject.

question:
Select the sentence that contains the homonym of the highlighted word.

 

The troops were ordered not to desert the outpost under any circumstances.
option_1: Many recruits desert their units during a prolonged conflict.
option_2: The caravan crossed the desert in a little over twelve days.
option_3: He would never desert a friend in difficulty.
option_4: Villagers began to desert the settlement after the third failed monsoon.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The caravan crossed the desert in a little over twelve days.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homonym is a word with the same spelling but an entirely different meaning. In the given sentence, desert is a verb meaning to abandon a post or duty. (छोड़ देना, भाग जाना)

 

• In Option 2, desert is a noun meaning a barren, sandy region receiving very little rainfall. (रेगिस्तान) — a completely different sense, and therefore the homonym.
◦ Note the shift of stress as well: the verb is de-SERT, the noun is DE-sert.

 

• The remaining options all use desert in the same sense as the highlighted word — abandoning something — so none of them qualifies.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: desert their units — to abandon military service; identical in meaning to the given sentence.

 

• Option 3: desert a friend — to abandon someone who needs help; the same sense used figuratively.

 

• Option 4: desert the settlement — to leave a place empty; again the same sense.

 

NOTE

 

• Do not confuse desert (to abandon / a dry region) with dessert (मीठा व्यंजन), the sweet course at the end of a meal, which has a double ‘s’.

 

• Other frequently tested homonyms: bank, bark, bat, fair, lie, match, pupil, right, spring, volume.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

We are taught to regard forgetting as the failure of memory, a leak in an otherwise sound vessel. Yet a mind that retained everything would not be a superior mind; it would be an unusable one. To remember is not to store but to select, and every act of selection is at the same time an act of discarding. The past does not survive in us as an archive faithfully preserved; it survives as a palimpsest, each recollection written over the faint traces of the last, quietly altered by the hand that copies it.

 

This is not a defect in our design but the very condition of thought. Generalisation, judgement, even forgiveness depend upon a merciful blurring of detail. The man who cannot forget an insult cannot forgive it; the scholar who cannot forget particulars cannot arrive at a principle. Literature understood long before psychology conceded it that total recall is a curse: Borges imagined a man who could perceive every leaf of every tree and was, for that reason, incapable of thinking, since thought demands the courage to lose detail.

 

Societies remember in the same manner. A nation that recalled every grievance in its full original heat could not compose a common future; the gradual softening of memory is what allows adversaries to become neighbours. This is not the same as erasure, which is dishonest and finally dangerous, for a wound concealed festers longer than one confessed. Between the tyranny of total recall and the violence of enforced amnesia lies the harder discipline of remembering well — keeping what instructs, releasing what merely wounds.

 

Which of the following best completes the analogy: Remembering is to selection as forgetting is to — ?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Discarding.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The analogy is drawn straight from the first paragraph: to remember is not to store but to select, and every act of selection is at the same time an act of discarding.

 

• The two halves of that sentence pair the terms exactly — remembering ↔ selection, and therefore forgetting ↔ discarding. The relationship asked for is one of definition, not of consequence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Erasure is explicitly rejected by the author in the last paragraph — forgetting is said not to be the same as erasure, which is called dishonest and dangerous.

 

• Option 3: Distortion describes what happens to a memory as it is rewritten (the palimpsest image), not what forgetting is.

 

• Option 4: Repetition has no basis anywhere in the passage.

 

NOTE

 

• In analogy-based comprehension questions, locate the single sentence in which both terms of the given pair appear together. The missing term is almost always its grammatical partner in that same sentence.

This is not the same as erasure, which is dishonest and finally dangerous, for a wound concealed festers longer than one confessed. Between the tyranny of total recall and the violence of enforced amnesia lies the harder discipline of remembering well — keeping what instructs, releasing what merely wounds.

 

Based on the passage, what can be reasonably inferred about the author’s view of forgetting?
option_1: It is a defect that a well-trained mind can overcome
option_2: It is a necessary partner of meaningful remembering
option_3: It is indistinguishable from the deliberate erasure of the past
option_4: It prevents societies from learning anything from their history
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. It is a necessary partner of meaningful remembering.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The author states that a mind retaining everything would be unusable, and that forgetting is not a defect in our design but the very condition of thought.

 

• The supporting examples all point the same way — forgiveness, generalisation and the forming of principles are each said to depend on a merciful blurring of detail. Forgetting is thus presented as what makes remembering useful, not as its enemy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reverses the argument: the author denies that forgetting is a defect at all, so there is nothing to “overcome”.

 

• Option 3 ignores the explicit distinction the author draws between forgetting and erasure.

 

• Option 4 contradicts the closing lines, which recommend keeping what instructs — that is, learning from the past.

 

NOTE

 

• An inference must be supported by the passage but not stated word for word. Options that exaggerate (“indistinguishable”, “nothing at all”) or reverse the author’s stand are the standard traps.

This is not the same as erasure, which is dishonest and finally dangerous, for a wound concealed festers longer than one confessed. Between the tyranny of total recall and the violence of enforced amnesia lies the harder discipline of remembering well — keeping what instructs, releasing what merely wounds.

 

What is the author’s primary purpose in writing this passage?
option_1: To describe recent scientific research on human memory
option_2: To argue that forgetting is essential to clear thought and to social peace
option_3: To warn nations against concealing uncomfortable chapters of their history
option_4: To compare the memory of individuals with that of institutions
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To argue that forgetting is essential to clear thought and to social peace.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage is argumentative, not descriptive. It opens by challenging a common assumption (that forgetting is a failure) and then defends the opposite position.

 

• The argument moves along two tracks that together give the purpose:
◦ the individual — judgement, generalisation and forgiveness require the loss of detail;
◦ the collective — the softening of grievance is what allows former adversaries to live as neighbours.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is wrong because no research, study or finding is described; psychology is mentioned only in passing.

 

• Option 3 picks up a single subordinate remark about erasure and treats it as the whole purpose.

 

• Option 4 names a comparison the passage does make, but that comparison serves the argument rather than being its aim.

 

NOTE

 

• For “primary purpose” questions, ask what the passage is trying to prove, not what it happens to mention. Options built on one paragraph alone are too narrow to be the answer.

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Contemplative means thoughtful, reflective and given to serious consideration of a subject. (चिंतनशील)

 

• The tone is set by the kind of language used throughout — measured generalisations (to remember is not to store but to select), an extended image (the palimpsest), a literary illustration and a balanced closing judgement. The author reasons rather than reacts.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Accusatory (आरोप लगाने वाला): the passage blames no person or group; even enforced amnesia is criticised in general terms.

 

• Option 3: Flippant (उच्छृंखल, गैर-गंभीर): treating a serious subject lightly — the opposite of the sustained seriousness here.

 

• Option 4: Indifferent (उदासीन): unconcerned; but the author clearly cares, recommending a definite “discipline of remembering well”.

 

NOTE

 

• Judge tone from vocabulary and sentence rhythm, not from the subject matter. A serious subject may still be treated satirically, and a light subject solemnly.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

We are taught to regard forgetting as the failure of memory, a leak in an otherwise sound vessel. Yet a mind that retained everything would not be a superior mind; it would be an unusable one. To remember is not to store but to select, and every act of selection is at the same time an act of discarding. The past does not survive in us as an archive faithfully preserved; it survives as a palimpsest, each recollection written over the faint traces of the last, quietly altered by the hand that copies it.

 

This is not a defect in our design but the very condition of thought. Generalisation, judgement, even forgiveness depend upon a merciful blurring of detail. The man who cannot forget an insult cannot forgive it; the scholar who cannot forget particulars cannot arrive at a principle. Literature understood long before psychology conceded it that total recall is a curse: Borges imagined a man who could perceive every leaf of every tree and was, for that reason, incapable of thinking, since thought demands the courage to lose detail.

 

Societies remember in the same manner. A nation that recalled every grievance in its full original heat could not compose a common future; the gradual softening of memory is what allows adversaries to become neighbours. This is not the same as erasure, which is dishonest and finally dangerous, for a wound concealed festers longer than one confessed. Between the tyranny of total recall and the violence of enforced amnesia lies the harder discipline of remembering well — keeping what instructs, releasing what merely wounds.

 

In the context of the passage, what does the word *palimpsest* most likely mean?
option_1: A sealed record that cannot be altered once written
option_2: A surface written on afresh, with the earlier writing still faintly visible
option_3: A deliberate falsification of an official document
option_4: An inherited instinct that survives without conscious effort
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A surface written on afresh, with the earlier writing still faintly visible.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage supplies its own definition immediately after the word: each recollection is written over the faint traces of the last, and is altered by the hand that copies it. That is precisely a palimpsest.

 

• Historically, a palimpsest is a manuscript page — usually parchment — from which earlier writing has been scraped off so that it can be used again, the older text remaining dimly legible underneath. (मिटाकर फिर से लिखी गई पाण्डुलिपि)

 

• The image is deliberately contrasted with the archive faithfully preserved in the previous line — memory overwrites, an archive does not.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes exactly what the author says memory is not — a faithfully preserved archive.

 

• Option 3 imports the idea of dishonesty, which the passage attaches to erasure, not to the palimpsest.

 

• Option 4 confuses the image with instinct or heredity, ideas absent from the passage.

 

NOTE

 

• For “word in context” questions, ignore any half-remembered dictionary meaning until you have read the clause immediately before and after the word; the passage nearly always explains it.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

The members of the committee are discussing about the proposal since Monday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. have been discussing.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Two separate errors have to be corrected together:
◦ ‘Discuss’ is a transitive verb and takes a direct object without any preposition — we discuss a proposal, never discuss about a proposal;
◦ the time expression ‘since Monday’ fixes a starting point, and an action begun in the past and still continuing requires the present perfect continuous.

 

• The subject is the members (plural), so the auxiliary is have, giving have been discussing.
◦ Corrected sentence: The members of the committee have been discussing the proposal since Monday.

 

• Beware of the intervening phrase of the committee; the verb agrees with members, not with committee.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 merely exchanges one wrong preposition for another and keeps the wrong tense.

 

• Option 3 retains about and uses the singular has with a plural subject.

 

• Option 4 is the past continuous, which cannot be used with since for an action still in progress.

 

NOTE

 

• Verbs that take no preposition after them: discuss, describe, enter, marry, resemble, reach, order, attack, accompany, comprise. Verbs that need one: listen to, wait for, apply for, rely on, insist on.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

He is one of those officers who is always willing to work beyond office hours.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. are always willing.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the pattern ‘one of those + plural noun + who/that …’, the relative pronoun who refers back to the plural noun immediately before it — here officers — and therefore takes a plural verb.
◦ Corrected sentence: He is one of those officers who are always willing to work beyond office hours.

 

• Test it by rephrasing: Of those officers who are always willing to work beyond office hours, he is one. The plural verb becomes obvious.

 

• Distinguish this from ‘one of the + plural noun’ without a relative clause, where the main verb stays singular: One of the officers is on leave.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 is singular and also shifts the sentence into the past without reason.

 

• Option 3 puts a stative adjective (willing) into a continuous form, which is unidiomatic.

 

• Option 4 is singular; besides, always with a general habit takes the simple present, not the present perfect.

 

NOTE

 

• Compare the two structures carefully, as SSC sets them against each other:
◦ He is one of the best players who have represented the state. (plural)
◦ He is the only one of the players who has represented the state. (singular — only one changes the reference)

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

He said to me, “Where have you kept the spare keys?”
option_1: He asked me where had I kept the spare keys.
option_2: He said to me that where I had kept the spare keys.
option_3: He asked me where I had kept the spare keys.
option_4: He asked me where have you kept the spare keys.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. He asked me where I had kept the spare keys.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Three changes are required when an interrogative sentence is reported:
◦ the reporting verb said to becomes asked;
◦ for a wh-question, the question word itself (where) acts as the connective — that is never used;
◦ the interrogative order is replaced by the statement order: subject + verb, and the question mark is dropped.

 

• The reporting verb is in the past, so the tense moves back one step: have kept → had kept. The pronoun you (addressed to the speaker, me) becomes I.
◦ Indirect: He asked me where I had kept the spare keys.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 retains the interrogative order (had I kept) in the reported clause.

 

• Option 2 wrongly inserts that along with the question word and keeps said to instead of asked.

 

• Option 4 changes neither the tense nor the pronoun, reproducing the question as it stood.

 

NOTE

 

• For yes/no questions, use if or whether instead of a question word: He said to me, “Are you ready?” → He asked me whether I was ready.

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

The old man asked the boy whether he could help him carry the sack.
option_1: “Can you help me carry the sack?” the old man asked the boy.
option_2: “Could he help him carry the sack?” said the old man to the boy.
option_3: “Will you help me to carrying the sack?” the old man asked the boy.
option_4: “You can help me carry the sack,” the old man told the boy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. “Can you help me carry the sack?” the old man asked the boy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The connective whether signals a yes/no question in the original speech, so the direct form must be a question ending in a question mark, enclosed in inverted commas.

 

• Working backwards from the reported clause:
◦ could → can (the back-shift caused by the past reporting verb is undone);
◦ he → you (the person addressed, i.e. the boy);
◦ him → me (the speaker, i.e. the old man);
◦ the statement order is restored to the interrogative order: Can you help …?

 

• Direct: “Can you help me carry the sack?” the old man asked the boy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 leaves the reported pronouns he and him unchanged, so it is not genuine direct speech.

 

• Option 3 replaces could with will and adds an ungrammatical to carrying.

 

• Option 4 turns the question into a statement, which contradicts asked … whether.

 

NOTE

 

• While converting indirect to direct speech, always restore: the inverted commas, the capital letter at the start of the quotation, the original tense, the original pronouns, and the correct end punctuation (? for questions, ! for exclamations).

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The small railway platform on the outskirts of the town had stood unused for nearly thirty years.

 

A. Word spread, and passengers waiting for the evening train began leaving books of their own on the benches.

 

B. A retired station master started stacking his personal collection there, simply because the shelves of his house had run out.

 

C. What had begun as one man’s private habit had quietly become the district’s busiest reading room.

 

D. Within two years the platform held more than four thousand volumes.

 

S2. The shelves are looked after today by the townspeople themselves, without a single paid librarian.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. B-A-D-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – A – D – C – S2, and the paragraph follows a clear situation → first act → spread → result → summing-up order.

 

• S1 presents the situation: an unused platform.
◦ B supplies the first act — the station master starts stacking books there, and the adverb there points straight back to the platform in S1.
◦ A follows with “Word spread”, which can only refer to news of what B describes; books of their own also presupposes the first collection.
◦ D gives the cumulative result — four thousand volumes — which is possible only after others too had begun contributing in A.
◦ C is the summing-up sentence (What had begun as one man’s private habit …) and leads naturally into S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (A-B-D-C) opens with “Word spread” before anything has happened that could spread.

 

• Option 2 (B-D-A-C) places the total of four thousand volumes before the townspeople begin contributing.

 

• Option 4 (D-B-A-C) begins with the outcome and leaves the collection unexplained.

 

NOTE

 

• In rearrangement questions, the sentence containing a summing-up phrase (What had begun as …, In this way …, Thus …) is almost always the last of the jumbled sentences.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The tomato was grown in Europe for nearly two centuries before anyone there dared to eat it.

 

A. Only in the eighteenth century, when Italian cooks began using it freely, did the suspicion finally dissolve.

 

B. The reason lay in its botany, for it belonged to the same family as the poisonous nightshade.

 

C. Within a few generations the once-dreaded plant had become inseparable from European cooking.

 

D. Gardeners therefore raised it as an ornamental curiosity, admiring the fruit but never tasting it.

 

S2. Few foods illustrate so neatly how quickly fear can turn into fondness.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. B-D-A-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – D – A – C – S2, and the paragraph moves from puzzle → reason → consequence → turning point → outcome.

 

• S1 raises the puzzle: why was a cultivated plant never eaten?
◦ B answers it directly — “The reason lay in its botany” — and must therefore come first among the jumbled sentences.
◦ D begins with “Gardeners therefore …”, and therefore can only follow the reason given in B.
◦ A marks the turning point (Only in the eighteenth century … did the suspicion dissolve), reversing the situation described in D.
◦ C states the outcome of that reversal — the plant becomes inseparable from European cooking — leading straight into S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (D-B-A-C) places therefore before the reason it depends on.

 

• Option 3 (B-A-D-C) allows the suspicion to dissolve in A and then revives it in D.

 

• Option 4 (A-B-D-C) opens with the turning point, so the reader meets “the suspicion” before learning what it was.

 

NOTE

 

• Connectives fix the order. Therefore, thus, consequently must follow a cause; only when/only after signal a reversal in the middle; and a sentence beginning with “The reason lay in …” must follow the statement whose reason it supplies.
